sentences.text: Nils's grandmother taught him to read them, over about two summers, in the way she taught everything, which was by standing behind him saying nothing until he asked a question worth answering.
The first question he asked that she thought was worth answering was, at eight, why the rings on one side were wider than on the other.

She said that the tree grows more on the side that has more light and that this is called reaction wood and that if he wanted to know which way was south in that forest without a compass he could look at a stump.
Nothing tells you what year you are looking at.
But they are not all alike, and once you can see the differences you can work outwards from the bark, which is now, and count.
A wide pale ring is a good summer.
A narrow dark one is a bad one.

There are two rings in the birch that are so thin they are almost a line, and those are 1867 and 1868, and every tree of that age in northern Sweden has them and every forester in that country knows what they are.
There is a black band in the pine by the marsh at about the sixtieth ring in and it goes right round, and that is fire.

And there is one, in the big spruce at the top of the ridge, about a hundred and twenty rings in, where the wood on one side goes suddenly thick and buckled for four or five years and then settles down — which means that in about 1904 something took the top off that tree, or leaned another tree against it, and it spent five years correcting and then got on with its life.
Nils could find that one in the dark by his fifteenth birthday.
His grandmother had a name for it — *det stygga året*, the bad year — and Nils has never found anybody else in Västerbotten who uses that phrase and suspects she made it up.
Everything he has described is in the wood of every tree in that forest and you can see all of it by cutting one down and looking at the stump, which foresters do every day of the week.
The only strange part is that you can see it from outside, through a hole the width of a fist, in a tree that is standing up and alive and has another two hundred years in it.
